query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The phase transition in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by a surface premelting mechanism. That is, reduced atomic coordination at the nanoparticle surfaces raises the local atomic mobility, so melting initiates at the surface and propagates inward, with smaller particles (having higher surface‐to‐volume ratios) beginning their transition at lower temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, crystalline FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with uniform composition, varying in size to provide different surface-to-volume ratios.
generation.intervention: A controlled molecular-dynamics heating simulation comparing nanoparticles of different sizes, keeping the heating rate and inert atmosphere constant.
generation.conditions: Identical heating conditions (similar heating rate, inert environment) across a series of nanoparticle sizes (e.g., 5 nm vs. 20 nm).
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoparticle surface, where atoms have fewer neighboring atoms (lower coordination), leading to enhanced atomic mobility and lowered local melting barriers.
generation.mechanism: Reduced coordination at nanoparticle surfaces increases local atomic vibrations and mobility, triggering surface premelting. This surface disorder then propagates inwards, causing a progressive phase transition. This effect is more pronounced in smaller particles due to their relatively larger surface areas.
generation.predicted_outcome: Smaller nanoparticles will show an earlier onset of surface disorder (indicative of premelting) at temperatures tens of degrees lower than larger nanoparticles. The disorder will initiate at surfaces and corners and propagate inward during heating.
generation.baseline: A uniformly solid, crystalline state at ambient temperatures before heating.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under controlled, moderate heating rates and inert atmosphere conditions; extreme heating rates or compositional inhomogeneities might introduce additional effects not covered by this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature depression and kinetics of the phase change are simulation-dependent and may vary with precise nanoparticle shapes and local compositional fluctuations.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform molecular-dynamics heating simulations on nanoparticles of different sizes (for example, 5 nm, 10 nm and 20 nm) under identical heating conditions. Monitor the temperature at which surface disorder (premelting) begins and trace the spatial progression of the disorder from the surface into the core.
measurements: Onset temperature of surface disorder using atomic displacement metrics (e.g., RMSD)
Spatial progression of structural disorder via radial distribution functions
Time-resolved snapshots tracking the migration of disordered regions from the surface inward
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulations do not show a systematic change with particle size — specifically, if surface premelting is not observed to initiate at lower temperatures in smaller nanoparticles or if melting starts uniformly rather than at the surface — then the hypothesis would be falsified.
